quick: VTE prophylaxis 1432 IU anti-Xa SC once daily (normal risk); treatment 143 IU anti-Xa/kg/day in 2 SC doses
Subcutaneous injection; not related to meals
Studies suggest prophylactic doses can be used; use with caution
Use during breastfeeding not advised (data lacking; oral absorption unlikely)
Contraindicated if CrCl <30 mL/min; caution and anti-Xa monitoring if moderate impairment
Use in hepatic impairment not studied; severe liver/pancreas impairment contraindicated
Platelet count (HIT), signs of bleeding, serum potassium, anti-Xa if needed
summary: Reviparin sodium (Clivarin) is a low molecular weight heparin (mean molecular weight ~3150-5150 Da) used for the prevention of venous thromboembolism in general and orthopaedic surgery and for the treatment of venous thrombosis. It is given subcutaneously: 1432 IU anti-Xa once daily for normal-risk surgical prophylaxis, 3436 IU once daily for high-risk (e.g., hip/knee replacement) prophylaxis, and 143 IU anti-Xa/kg/day in two divided doses (max 10,307 IU/day) for treatment of deep vein thrombosis. It is NOT FDA-approved; this monograph is based on the European SmPC (Clivarin). Like other LMWHs, it carries bleeding risk, must not be used interchangeably unit-for-unit with other heparins, can cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and (rarely) hyperkalaemia, and carries a risk of spinal/epidural haematoma with neuraxial anaesthesia. Protamine partially reverses its effect.
indications: Prevention of venous thromboembolism in general surgery and orthopaedic surgery
Treatment of venous thrombosis (deep vein thrombosis)

dosage.n: First injection 2 hours before surgery or when immobilised; usually 7-14 days in general surgery
First injection 12 hours before surgery; at least 14 days

dosage.d: 143 IU anti-Xa/kg/day in two SC injections (35-45 kg: 2863 IU BID; 46-60 kg: 3436 IU BID; >60 kg: 5153 IU BID); max 10,307 IU/day
dosage.n: Overlap with oral anticoagulant to target INR 2.0-3.0; give for at least 5-7 days

admin: For subcutaneous use only - do NOT give intramuscularly
Inject into a pinched skin fold of the abdominal wall (between umbilicus and iliac crest) or front of the thigh; insert and withdraw the needle perpendicularly
Do not aspirate before injection; single-use prefilled syringe (residual volume accounted for - do not expel the air bubble)
Do not mix with other injections or infusions
Avoid IM injections of other drugs during therapy (haematoma risk); note the needle cover contains latex
moa: Reviparin is a low molecular weight heparin obtained by fractionation of porcine heparin. It binds antithrombin and accelerates inactivation of activated coagulation factors, with a marked inhibitory action on factor Xa and comparatively low anti-factor IIa (thrombin) activity (anti-Xa:anti-IIa ratio ~3.6-6.1). This preferential factor Xa inhibition produces an antithrombotic effect during the early stages of coagulation with relatively less effect on overall clotting tests than unfractionated heparin.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to reviparin, any excipient, other LMWHs, or heparin; history of known or suspected immune-mediated heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (type II)
Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min)

Conditions with elevated bleeding risk: active haemorrhage, haemorrhagic diathesis, coagulation factor deficiency, severe thrombocytopenia, uncontrolled hypertension, bacterial/subacute endocarditis, active GI ulceration or haemorrhage, haemorrhagic stroke
Spinal, ear, or ophthalmological surgery and intraocular bleeding or injuries thereof; severe impairment of liver and pancreas function
Therapeutic-dose use during lumbar puncture or spinal/epidural anaesthesia
relative: Concomitant anticoagulants, antiplatelets, or NSAIDs (bleeding risk)
Moderate renal impairment (monitor anti-Xa) and the elderly
Diabetic retinopathy; conditions predisposing to hyperkalaemia (diabetes, CKD, potassium-sparing drugs)
monitor: Signs of bleeding and of spinal/epidural haematoma with neuraxial techniques
Serum potassium (hyperkalaemia risk, especially beyond ~7 days)
Anti-Xa levels in moderate renal impairment or therapeutic dosing when indicated

preg: Controlled studies in pregnancy have not been performed. In second- and third-trimester studies and ex vivo perfused human placentas, placental passage of reviparin could not be demonstrated; in a clinical study of more than 50 pregnant women with recurrent miscarriage, prophylactic-dose reviparin throughout pregnancy appeared safe, and animal studies showed no harmful reproductive effects. Caution should be exercised when prescribing to pregnant women.
lact: Information on the passage of reviparin into breast milk is not available, and oral absorption by an infant is unlikely; nonetheless the use of reviparin during breastfeeding is not advised per the SmPC.
renal: Use with caution in mild to moderate renal impairment; reviparin is contraindicated in severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min). With therapeutic doses in moderate impairment (CrCl 30-50 mL/min), consider monitoring anti-Xa levels (target ~0.5-1 U/mL at 3-4 hours after dosing). The elderly often have reduced renal function - use with care.
hepatic: Use of reviparin in hepatic impairment has not been studied. Severe impairment of liver (and pancreas) function is a contraindication because of bleeding risk.

major: Other anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors (e.g., aspirin, NSAIDs, oral anticoagulants) - potentiated bleeding risk; use with extreme caution
moderate: Drugs that raise serum potassium and potassium-sparing agents - additive hyperkalaemia risk
Dextran and other plasma expanders affecting platelet function
minor: Nitroglycerin infusions may reduce the effect of heparin
interactions.alcohol: No specific alcohol interaction is described in the SmPC.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor platelet count and serum potassium; may elevate serum transaminases (ALT, AST, gamma-GT). Anti-Xa is the appropriate assay (aPTT is relatively insensitive to LMWH).

common: Haemorrhage / subcutaneous haematoma and injection-site bleeding
Fever; pain in extremity; abnormal liver function tests
serious: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia type II with paradoxical thrombosis
Spinal or epidural haematoma with neuraxial anaesthesia (can cause prolonged/permanent paralysis)
rare: Skin necrosis at the injection site
Mild transient (type I) thrombocytopenia early in therapy
emergency: Signs of spinal/epidural haematoma (back pain, leg numbness/weakness, bladder/bowel dysfunction)

monitoring: Platelet count before therapy, on day 1, then regularly every 3-4 days and at the end of therapy (HIT surveillance)
Serum electrolytes (potassium) in at-risk patients, especially if treated beyond ~7 days
Neurologic signs of spinal/epidural haematoma in patients with neuraxial catheters
Anti-Xa activity in moderate renal impairment or therapeutic dosing when indicated
counsel: This is a blood thinner given as an injection under the skin of the abdomen or thigh; learn proper technique and rotate sites
Watch for and report unusual bleeding or bruising, black or bloody stools, blood in urine, or severe nosebleeds
If you have spinal anaesthesia or a spinal procedure, report back pain, leg numbness/weakness, or loss of bladder/bowel control immediately
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, especially aspirin, NSAIDs, and other blood thinners
The needle cover contains latex - tell your team if you have a latex allergy
pk: Anticoagulant (anti-Xa) effect develops after subcutaneous absorption
Plasma anti-Xa peaks about 3 hours after subcutaneous injection
Elimination half-life approximately 3 hours (independent of dose)
Once- or twice-daily dosing depending on indication; bioavailability ~95% subcutaneously
Store per the SmPC/manufacturer (controlled room temperature; do not freeze the prefilled syringe)
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - this monograph is based on the European SmPC (Clivarin); reviparin is a porcine-derived LMWH
Cannot be used interchangeably unit-for-unit with unfractionated heparin or other LMWHs (different units and potency)
Contraindicated if CrCl <30 mL/min; monitor anti-Xa in moderate renal impairment and consider it for therapeutic dosing
Risks of spinal/epidural haematoma (timing around neuraxial catheters), HIT (monitor platelets), and hyperkalaemia (aldosterone suppression)
Protamine partially reverses anti-Xa and fully neutralises anti-IIa - about 17.5 mg protamine per 1432 IU (1 mg neutralises ~81.8 IU anti-Xa); bolus not to exceed 50 mg
missed: If a scheduled subcutaneous dose is missed, contact the prescriber; generally take it as soon as remembered unless it is close to the next dose, in which case skip it - do not double the dose. Do not stop anticoagulation without medical advice.
overdose: Overdose causes hypocoagulability and increased bleeding risk. Minor bleeding/haematoma at normal doses usually does not require stopping treatment. For significant bleeding, slow intravenous protamine partially neutralises anti-Xa activity and fully neutralises anti-IIa activity; about 17.5 mg protamine neutralises a 1432 IU dose (1 mg protamine neutralises ~81.8 IU anti-Xa), with the bolus not exceeding 50 mg and the LMWH half-life taken into account.
